title: Dozens of illegal vendors swarm Brooklyn Bridge, crowd out licensed counterparts including disabled vets
text:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Dozens of unlicensed vendors have illegally swarmed the Brooklyn Bridge to hawk cheap New York City souvenirs and fruit cups — while their licensed competition, including disabled veterans, say they’re being pushed out and unable to make a living.

The Post counted roughly 42 vendors across the historic span on Sunday and spotted one brazenly spreading out dozens of New York canvas bags directly in front of a “no vending allowed” sign.

The illicit hawkers peddled Big Apple-themed tchotchkes, including $1 NYC magnets and $5 hats. An 11-year-old girl even sold a Post reporter a $1 bottle of water before pointing up the bridge and stating her mom was “selling mangos.”

The disorderly scene has frustrated local licensed merchants, including disabled veterans who said they are unable to compete with their unlicensed counterparts.

Sammy, a 48-year-old licensed ice cream vendor and disabled veteran who has worked near City Hall for decades, said the illicit vendors returned around October 2025, but claimed, “the chaos exploded under Mamdani.”

“It started under Adams because he didn’t give a f–k,” he said of the end of former Mayor Eric Adams’ term.

“They’re illegal vendors. They’re there, and they’re back,” Sammy said. “They’re causing chaos. They’re costing the city money. Cops are chasing them.”

Sammy said police occasionally issue tickets, but the fines appear to do little to curb the peddlers who rack up profits by selling illegally.

The Post witnessed several sellers flee the bridge as a pair of cops patrolled the expanse.

“They give tickets, but they give little stupid $20 tickets, $50 tickets. But he’s going to make $1,000 illegally, so what’s a $20 ticket?”

The turf wars amongst the vendors have also turned violent.

Last week, Sammy was left with scratches all over his arms after breaking up a fight between mango sellers.

“They’re all fighting with each other. The illegal mango [sellers] are cutting each other up, scratching,” Sammy said.

“They were fighting. I tried to get in between them to stop them from fighting. The wife jumps on me while I’m trying to hold her husband from getting hit by the other five guys. The next thing you know, they’re all punching me and scratching me,” he added.

“I’m doing the police work, I’m doing the Parks Department work, and I’m an ice cream guy.”

In January 2024, Adams followed through on a promise to boot the “packed like sardines” vendors from the Brooklyn Bridge to the relief of pedestrians.

A rule went into effect that January to prohibit vending on pedestrian walkways and bike lanes on bridges and bridge approaches.

The regulation was slated to affect all Big Apple crossings — but was specifically created to target the Brooklyn Bridge after the 1.14-mile-long historic landmark turned into an open-air free-for-all.

But Sammy blasted Mamdani for not doing enough to stop the peddlers whose low prices he claims have forced other souvenir shops to shutter.

“It’s hurting everybody … the stores, the businesses over here. It’s hurting everybody. The people over here are all disabled veterans,” he said of the licensed vendors outside of City Hall, many of whom are unable to set up because the illegal vendors get there at the crack of dawn and “beat everyone to the spot.”

“Mamdani is new, but the [eight] months he’s been in, nothing has changed over there. The cops are not allowed to bother them, and if they arrest somebody, the DA releases them.”

A 41-year-old disabled veteran and US Marine who was discharged in 2008 also told The Post that there are now more than 100 unlicensed vendors on the bridge at times.

“Us being disabled veterans and having a license means nothing over there now because if I go over there, they’re going to kick me out. But they’re not kicking [illegal vendors] out now,” said the licensed vendor, who declined to give his name for fear of retaliation.

He claimed he went to court and the city told him he could not vend on the bridge because it was a “national security” issue.

“These people who just jumped the border, there’s no national security for them,” he said of the unlicensed vendors.

“Before they got rid of all the vendors, there were about 60 – 80 vendors…Now there’s about 120 vendors.”

“If you start from Manhattan side [of the bridge] all the way to Brooklyn side, it’s full of vendors on the floor, and they’re not confiscating nobody’s merchandise. They’re not doing any enforcement, but the moment I go over there, they want to come and harass me and take my merchandise,” he said of the NYPD.

“This is pretty much my livelihood,” he said. “We just want equal enforcement, that’s all.”
